title: Multiorbital driving of quantum geometric nonlinear transport in oxide interfaces
summary: Quantum geometry plays a relevant role in determining the intrinsic non-linear transport properties of low-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the quantum geometric contribution to the non-linear conductivity in $\text{SrTiO}_3$-based two-dimensional electron gases, comparing the prototypical (001) and (111) crystallographic interface orientations. Using a multi-orbital tight-binding approach, we uncover the crucial role of the multiband electronic structure in determining the quantum-geometric contribution to nonlinear transport. In particular, we show how the hybridization of $t_{2g}$ orbitals near avoided band crossings shapes the momentum-space distribution of the band-normalized quantum metric and the resulting nonlinear conductivity. Furthermore, we reveal a strong dependence on crystal orientation: while the (001) interface exhibits sharp peak-and-dip features confined around Lifshitz transitions, the trigonal symmetry of the (111) interface promotes strong orbital mixing. Our results highlight how the interplay between orbital hybridization and crystallographic orientation gives rise to distinct quantum-geometric nonlinear transport responses in oxide interfaces.

title: Wireless readout and control of cavity magnon-polaritons via photonic modes delocalised across a gap
summary: In cavity magnonics, photon-magnon hybridisation is typically detected by measuring the cavity response (i.e. measuring cavity resonance shifts through its reflection or transmission spectra). While a large body of work in the field has focused on three-dimensional cavities, a variety of two-dimensional resonators have also been explored as hosts for photonic modes due to their compatibility with on-chip integration. Nevertheless, the readout approach remains largely unchanged. Here, we demonstrate remote excitation and readout of cavity magnon-polaritons using two spatially separated, wirelessly coupled ring resonators. Through inductive coupling, energy is transferred between the resonators, enabling the magnonic system to be excited by one resonator while its hybrid-mode spectrum is detected through measurements of the other. We demonstrate wireless readout of cavity magnon-polaritons at separations ranging from millimetres to centimetres, identifying their characteristic response in the remotely measured spectrum. This establishes wireless resonator coupling as a route to remote interrogation of hybrid photon-magnon systems.

title: Spherical HgTe nanocrystal: a multi-band effective mass study
summary: The size-quantized energies, eigenstates, and optical selection rules in a spherical HgTe nanocrystal are studied by solving the multi-band effective-mass equations analytically. The six-band Kane model, involving both the $Γ_{6}$ and $Γ_{8}$ bands within the spherical approximation, is employed in the derivation. The eigenstates can be classified by both the total angular momentum and the parity. As the nanocrystal radius varies, crossings occur not only between electron and hole energy levels but also among the hole levels themselves. The lowest two electron states (in each spin subspace) are surface states, one with even parity and the other with odd parity. The optical selection rules consist of two parts, namely, the parity selection and the angular momentum selection.

title: Quantum Hall Effect in a 3D Cross-Dimensional Quantum Anomalous Hall System
summary: We systematically investigate cross-dimensional transport and the resulting quantum Hall effect in 3D quantum anomalous Hall effect systems, which are constructed by coupling two Weyl-semimetal Hamiltonians. Our study unveils that the system hosts highly anisotropic surface states and chiral modes, leading to rich quantum Hall responses. Crucially, we clarify how magnetic fields applied along three high-symmetry directions dictate the evolution of the Chern numbers, chiral modes, and Hall responses. We discover that chiral modes along different directions can originate from distinct mechanisms, giving rise to various magnetic modulation characteristics. Furthermore, we unveil the breakdown of the conventional Chern-number-based bulk-boundary correspondence under magnetic fields, where the Chern numbers alone fail to fully characterize the evolution of the chiral states. This anomalous behavior is attributed to the unique momentum-space distributions of surface bands. These insights are further validated numerically through multi-terminal Hall transport simulations. Our findings expand the understanding of magnetic-field-driven mechanisms in 3D topological systems and provide deeper insights into the interplay between quantized Hall effects and Chern numbers in 3D systems.

title: Observation of collective flatbands in hybrid Mie-grating THz metasurfaces
comment: 12 pages of main text with 5 figures; 20 pages of Supporting Information with 12 supplementary figures. This work elucidates the microscopic origins of collective photonic band structures through multipolar interactions within the Mie-tronics framework
summary: We propose a novel type of functional metasurfaces created by a hybridization of Mie resonators with high-index optical gratings. We demonstrate that such hybrid metasurfaces possess flatbands characterized by zero group velocity and strong energy localization. We experimentally observe the flatbands in free-standing terahertz (THz) metasurfaces, where dielectric interconnections between Mie resonators, forming the grating, mediate multipolar hybridization and provide a geometric control over collective resonances. Our THz near-field measurements with a dipole excitation uncover long-lived coherent oscillations associated with the quasi-flat magnetic-dipolar resonant modes, while a spatial mapping resolves the resonant electromagnetic response across the dielectric interconnections. We vary the grating width continuously to tune the hybrid magnetic-dipolar resonances and substantially enhance the quality factor (Q factor), while preserving the quasi-!atband dispersion. Complementary Bloch-resolved Purcell calculations reveal the substantial Purcell enhancement with increasing Q factor, followed by a trend towards saturation and highlighting the interplay between radiative confinement and local emitter-mode coupling. We believe our findings establish the engineering of dielectric interconnections in periodic lattices as a novel strategy for spectrally tuning high-Q flatbands in these metastructures, tailoring localized electromagnetic interactions in functional optical metasurfaces.

title: State-selective dynamical freezing in driven Rydberg atom chains
summary: Dynamical freezing, the near-complete suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies, offers a route to mitigating Floquet heating in periodically driven quantum systems. In interacting systems, however, the energy cost of each transition depends on the many-body configuration, so that the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. We study this dependence in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Using Floquet perturbation theory, we show that each spin flip is characterised by a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and that a state freezes only where the amplitudes of all its available flips vanish simultaneously. This picture accounts quantitatively for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing and for the response of entire families of initial states, which are sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a window of spacings bounded by interaction tails on one side and nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation on the other, outside of which the advantage of bi-frequency driving is lost. In the regime of large detuning amplitude, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.

title: Local Pressure Induced Quantum Dot to Ring Transition and Aharonov Bohm Effect in Reconfigurable MoTe2 Bilayers
summary: We demonstrate that local pressure provides an effective means of engineering reconfigurable quantum confinement in MoTe2 homobilayers. By applying a smooth, spatially varying pressure profile, we show that the confinement geometry can be continuously tuned from a conventional quantum dot to a quantum ring, with the emergence of annular confinement being a distinctive feature of AB-stacked bilayers. This crossover originates from the pressure-induced spatial modulation in the electronic parameters, which produces an off-center minimum in the effective confinement potential, thereby redistributing the ground-state probability density away from the center and giving rise to an annular confinement geometry. In the quantum-ring regime, a perpendicular magnetic field gives rise to a flux-periodic energy spectrum and persistent currents, providing characteristic signatures of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. By coupling the pressure-induced quantum ring to source and drain leads, we further demonstrate pronounced Aharonov-Bohm conductance oscillations, accompanied by real-space current patterns exhibiting constructive and destructive interference at integer and half-integer magnetic flux quanta, respectively. These findings establish locally pressurized MoTe2 bilayers as a lithography-free platform for reconfigurable quantum confinement and realizing pressure-tunable Aharonov-Bohm interferometry in two dimensional materials.

title: Picojoule-level self-referencing with dual dispersive waves in thin-film lithium niobate
summary: We demonstrate pulse-energy-efficient f-2f self-referencing of telecom-band pulses in a monolithic thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguide that combines Kerr spectral broadening with quasi-phase-matched (QPM) second-harmonic generation (SHG). Dispersion engineering generates dual dispersive waves (DWs) near 1 and 2 um, placed symmetrically around the pump to reduce the required spectral broadening. With an on-chip pulse energy of only 16.8 pJ, we detect a carrier-envelope-offset frequency (fceo) beatnote with a 32 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and we stabilize the fceo of an Er-fiber laser at 30 pJ, which is, to our knowledge, the lowest pulse energy reported for fceo stabilization at telecom wavelengths. Compared with an identical waveguide without poling, the QPM section enhances the beatnote SNR by 43 dB and reduces the required pulse energy fourfold. We further show that a mode-crossing DW, a chirped poling period, and a poled section aligned with the onset of DW generation to mitigate temporal walk-off are key to this performance.

title: Foliated surface codes for optimal skip-gate leakage correction
summary: Skip-gate leakage --- such as atom loss in neutral-atom arrays or trapped ions, or photon loss in superconducting dual-rail qubits --- takes a qubit out of its computational subspace and removes subsequent gates acting on it. If leakage is only detectable end-of-the-line at qubit measurement, error correction circuits must be designed to periodically measure all qubits, as in SWAP-based circuits and foliation. We show that the best SWAP-based surface code, although optimal against space-like skip-gate leakage errors, is suboptimal against time-like leakage errors. By optimal, we mean that the code corrects as many leakage errors as it can detect. Remarkably, we find that the foliated surface code is optimal against both space- and time-like error configurations. We support our findings with numerical simulations. Under two-qubit gate leakage with probability 0.5%, foliation suppresses time-like errors in a distance-4 rotated stability experiment by 1380(50) per two added rounds, compared to 63(1) for the best SWAP-based circuit. In memory, the two are comparable. Under an experimentally motivated neutral-atom noise model, we find that foliation outperforms SWAP-based circuits in stability for both rotated and unrotated code geometries. This holds true for a parameter sweep that takes the neutral-atom noise model from being dominated by computational errors to atom loss. Interestingly, a SWAP-based circuit for unrotated code memory performs best when computational noise dominates over loss. Our work motivates co-designing error correction circuits with logical operations: preferring foliation when time-like errors dominate and SWAP-based circuits when space-like errors dominate.

title: Floquet-Induced Valley Polarization and Topological Phases in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Heterostructures
summary: We theoretically investigate twisted bilayer graphene (tTBG) heterostructures subjected to circularly polarized light. Inversion symmetry is broken through the combined application of an out-of-plane electric field and the incorporation of insulating substrates, enabling precise control of the valley degrees of freedom and associated topological phases. We identify a regime in which the valley degeneracy is lifted: one valley retains a gapless, linear Dirac-like dispersion, whereas the other develops a finite band gap and becomes electronically inactive. The interplay between Floquet driving and inversion-symmetry breaking induces topological phase transitions characterized by Chern numbers C = -2, C = -1, and C = 0, together with the emergence of perfectly valley-polarized domain-wall channels. Furthermore, magnetic asymmetry arising from proximity to adjacent two-dimensional ferromagnetic contacts enables spin-valley filtering. These findings establish the potential of graphene-based heterostructures as highly tunable systems for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom.

title: Cryogenic Luminescence Thermometry of Upconversion Micro- and Nanoparticles via Deep Learning
summary: Luminescence thermometry with single or optically trapped particles is hampered by weak signals that fluctuate with alignment, collection efficiency, and excitation conditions and, for $\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$-based probes, by the loss of sensitivity of the luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) at cryogenic temperatures. Here we use a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) to predict the temperature directly from single emission spectra of $\mathrm{NaYF}_4{:}\mathrm{Yb}^{3+},\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ micro- and nanoparticles between $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $105\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and compare it with the standard LIR under adverse conditions deliberately reproduced with particle ensembles. From $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the 1D-CNN reduces the single-spectrum mean absolute error from $5.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $1.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and keeps its temperature uncertainty nearly constant down to the lowest temperatures, where Stark-component features remain temperature dependent while the LIR loses its sensitivity. Under deliberate optical misalignment, its error increases only from $0.58\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $0.88\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, whereas that of the LIR rises from $1.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $3.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The same approach reaches sub-degree accuracy ($0.21\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) over a narrow temperature window and a single calibration valid across different pump powers and wavelengths. These results establish 1D-CNNs as robust single-shot thermometers and a step toward fast thermometry of single and trapped particles.

title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
comment: 41 pages, 25 figures, 9 tables, comments are welcome
summary: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.

title: Interface invariants of rhombohedral graphene with layer-dependent potentials and couplings
summary: Domain walls in the perpendicular bias of rhombohedral (ABC-stacked) graphene bind valley-resolved interface modes whose signed number is fixed by a bulk-difference invariant. We determine which values of this invariant are reachable when the layer potentials are arbitrary monotone profiles, as produced by screening, and when the interlayer couplings vary from bond to bond. Within the single-particle continuum model, the invariant of an $m$-layer stack equals the difference of occupied angular weights of the zero-momentum levels, which reduces the classification to the ordering of those levels. At equal coupling, nonlinear monotone potentials reproduce exactly the set of invariants of linear potentials, also under the requirement of a common energy gap: screening moves phase boundaries but creates no new invariant values. With bond-dependent coupling, we characterize all occupied configurations. The range of attainable invariants is unchanged, but the gaps inside it are filled, beginning at five layers. Reflection-symmetric stacks realize a large subfamily with a guaranteed common gap, and lower bounds on single-bulk gaps complete the set of invariants with a common global gap for five and six layers. Among the examples is an eight-layer domain wall defined purely by gates, whose number of co-propagating channels per valley switches from 8 to 16 as the gate strength increases. Exact transfer-matrix calculations of the interface spectrum reproduce every predicted signed crossing count. A norm bound gives the minimum spread of interlayer coupling compatible with a prescribed gap.

title: Inverse design of polarization-analyzing gratings
summary: Metasurface polarization analyzing gratings have attracted increasing interest for polarization management and sensing in optical systems. Traditional strategies for the design of these gratings are based on a formalism combining the Jones calculus with Fourier optics. While this approach has achieved notable success in numerous applications, its validity is restricted to the paraxial regime. Here we introduce a differentiable topology optimization framework for these gratings which is free of this constraint. We show that this framework can yield designs which outperform the traditional approach, especially at high angles. Additionally, we provide preliminary experimental validation to corroborate these results.

title: Comment on phase vortex lattices in neutron interferometry
summary: We present a phase-based theoretical description of the four-plate crystal neutron interferometer (LLLL geometry) originally introduced by Heinrich et al. [Z. Phys. B 72, 357 (1988)]. The LLLL interferometer can be interpreted as two coupled LLL interferometric loops that share partial beam paths, leading to characteristic interference phenomena beyond the standard three-plate configuration. Using a coherent beam-splitting model we derive the forward intensity in terms of loop phase sums and recover the cosine-sum structure reported in Refs.[1,2]. Based on these results we analyze the phase dependence of the forward beam in the presence of localized phase objects, such as wedges inserted into individual partial beams. In experiments presented in [2], the LLLL interferometer is used to generate a periodic array of intensity in two dimensions by which the authors claim to demonstrate a phase vortex grating of significant extrinsic orbital angular momentum (OAM). However, the same interference patterns are predicted by simulating a coherent superposition of {beam paths} along different interferometer loops and experiencing phase shifts in each loop due to two wedges that are perpendicular to each other, without assuming any neutron OAM.

title: Population of spin orbit-split-electron branches in semimetallic HgTe quantum wells
summary: We present the results of experimental studies on magnetoresistance, the Hall effect, and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations performed in gated heterostructures with HgTe-based gapless semiconductor quantum wells. We show that in quantum wells with widths corresponding to a semimetallic charge carrier spectrum, electrons, in contrast to the idealized model, populate both spin-orbit-split branches of the spectrum. This occurs regardless of whether the Fermi level lies exclusively in the conduction band or within the conduction-valence band overlap region.

title: Excited-state lifetime and decay mechanisms in erbium-doped ZBLAN using Variable Excited-State dual-Pump Analysis
summary: This work presents a new technique for measuring excited-state lifetimes of rare-earth ions. This technique is particularly powerful for states that are very short lived or have a low photon yield because their de-excitation pathways are dominated by non-radiative processes. The technique uses dual optical parametric oscillators, whose pulses are separated by a variable delay. It reconstructs the excited-state decay curve from a series of delayed fluorescence intensity spectra rather than directly recording the fluorescence decay as done in conventional time-resolved laser fluorescence spectroscopy. The power of the technique is demonstrated by measuring the lifetime of the short-lived $^4I_{9/2}$ level in Er$^{3+}$-doped ZBLAN, which is well-known for its low photon yield. The technique enables accurate measurement of its lifetime and suggests a new depopulating mechanism involving the $^4I_{9/2}$ level in ZBLAN glass. Its accuracy is validated by measuring the lifetime of the $^4F_{9/2}$ state achieving excellent agreement with conventional time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy measurements. The approach is well suited for measuring lifetimes ranging from the sub-microsecond to the millisecond range. It provides a versatile platform for investigating excited-state dynamics and energy-transfer processes in RE-doped materials.

title: Distant Bell States via Measured Spin Chain Dynamics
summary: Preparing distant qubits in Bell states is a core requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation. The nonequilibrium unitary dynamics of spin chains have been envisaged as a convenient quantum channel for intra-chip communications. Typically it establishes mixed entangled states between its remote ends, to be purified by entanglement distillation after several uses of the channel to obtain Bell states. Here we show how the establishment of entanglement via spin chain dynamics can be (a) sped up and (b) made to yield a pure entangled state after a single usage of the channel, which is upgradable to a Bell-state without the complexity of purification. To this end, we intersperse unitary evolution for some period with measurements on intermediary spins. We explore two different measurements: a measurement that post-selects for a ground state; and local measurements in the computational basis. We illustrate the mechanism with qubits coupled to the ends of a 1D $XY$ spin chain.

title: FlakeForge: automated lithography-ready device layout from optical images of exfoliated van der Waals flakes
summary: Fabricating a device from an exfoliated van der Waals flake requires finding a suitable flake under a microscope and designing its lithography layout by hand. We present FlakeForge, an open-source pipeline from raw optical images of a marker-patterned chip to a lithography-ready, multilayer design file. It scores flakes for device usability, aligns and scales each image from its markers, fits the user's device design to each selected flake's contour and connects every contact to a bond pad by a trace routed around all earlier devices, so no two overlap. Demonstrated on Hall bars and Little-Parks rings, it processed four chips in about half an hour, work that took an expert days. It runs fully unattended or pauses for user review. Adapting it to a new material, marker design or device dimensions requires only configuration, with no training data; a new device type requires only its geometry definition.

title: Anisoplanatic Blind Deconvolution using Phase Diversity
summary: Atmospheric turbulence distorts the wavefront of light from a distant scene and blurs its image. Over a field of view wider than the isoplanatic angle, the distortion varies with direction and evolves in time, so no single wavefront describes the blur. Multiframe blind deconvolution (MFBD) can recover the scene from measurements spread over a long acquisition, but falls short during fast imaging because of limited diversity across measurements. We present coded anisoplanatic blind deconvolution (CA-BD), in which a pupil-plane spatial light modulator (SLM) applies a different known phase code to every measurement, with no wavefront sensor or deformable mirror, so that the measurements carry diversity even within a short acquisition. A per-pixel single-layer estimator recovers the object and spatially varying phases from the coded measurements. In simulation, a Cramér-Rao bound analysis shows that under anisoplanatism direct imaging needs about 41 times the photons of coded imaging for equal phase precision in strong turbulence. At the stronger of two turbulence strengths, CA-BD outperforms tuned MFBD on average at every burst length. It reduces the phase mean squared error 3.5x for stationary turbulence and 2-3x for time-varying turbulence. Measurements taken within a few coherence times benefit most from the known coded SLM patterns, making faster SLMs the key to its full advantage in time-varying turbulence.

title: Tailored Magic States for Algorithmic Primitives
summary: Algorithmic primitives such as adders, multipliers, and Boolean logic typically contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates, whose decomposition into $T$ and $CCZ$ gates adds scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation addresses this difficulty for diagonal circuits at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy by jointly synthesizing and distilling their non-Clifford content. In this work, we develop a complementary, code-theoretic approach to synthillation. We introduce CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and give analytical rules that predict these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, we generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy. We classify the resulting resource states as canonical (such as $T$ or $CCZ$), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible, i.e., not reducible to a product of non-Clifford gates via Clifford operations and logical basis changes. Conversion into Encode-$T$-Decode factories built from these codes recover known synthillation resources and prepare magic states at higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy; we analyze them with a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives. We demonstrate that tailored magic factories give significant latency improvements at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume: at code distance $21$ with one factory per resource family, they reduce the latency of a $GF(2^{8})$ multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to $48\%$ and $38\%$, respectively, and the smallest tailored factory also lowers the occupied spacetime volume. CSS-TP codes thus connect code construction to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives.

title: Kinetic inductance of two-dimensional viscous electron fluid
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, to be published in JETP Letters
summary: Modern high-mobility two-dimensional electron systems are pure enough to manifest hydrodynamic regime of electron transport similar to dynamics of classical fluids. With the bulk scattering controlled by momentum-conserving electron-electron collisions, these novel hydrodynamic materials demonstrate systematic violation of conventional metallic behavior due to the Drude model in stationary electric transport. In this letter, we study the linear reactive AC response of 2D electron fluid in a narrow channel geometry and show that the essentially non-local viscous dissipation induces non-trivial size effect in it. In particular, kinetic inductance, which represents collective inertia of the entire electron fluid, is enhanced by non-uniform flow profile and, in contrast to diffusive transport, dominates the electrical impedance already in collisional regime by virtue of viscous skin effect. The onset of reactive behavior falls within the microwave frequency domain in the state-of-the-art 2D hydrodynamic conductors which makes them promising material system for applications in high-frequency electronics at elevated temperatures.

title: MCP-based EUV ptychography with physics-simulation-trained residual learning
summary: Microchannel-plate (MCP) detectors offer high gain for extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) experiments, but spatial blur and nonlinear response hinder quantitative diffraction imaging. Here, we present an MCP-based EUV ptychography system that combines detector hardware with physics-simulation-trained computational restoration. A residual-learning neural network trained on simulated detector degradation restores diffraction patterns without experimentally acquired training pairs. This preprocessing substantially improves image quality compared with reconstructions from uncorrected data under identical reconstruction settings. Single-harmonic imaging at $57$~nm yields an effective edge-response width of $1.08~μ$m, approaching the nominal diffraction-limited scale of the imaging geometry. The approach further enables wavelength-multiplexed imaging at $44.4$ and $57$~nm. By coupling high-gain detection with computational compensation, this system enables high-resolution, multi-harmonic EUV ptychography and offers a cost-effective alternative to scientific-grade EUV CCD detectors

title: Incompressible quantum information
summary: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

title: Sondheimer oscillations in Weyl semimetal films
summary: In conducting films subject to an out-of-plane magnetic field, electron motion between the surfaces gives rise to conductance oscillations periodic in magnetic field, known as Sondheimer oscillations. While this size effect has been investigated in conventional metals, its dependence on the Berry curvature of topological materials remains less explored. In this work, we extend the semiclassical Boltzmann description of Sondheimer oscillations to type-I Weyl semimetal films. We account for the Berry curvature, the orbital magnetic moment and the effect of the Zeeman coupling on the Fermi wavevector and the electronic group velocity. The Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment generate a beating pattern and chirping in the Sondheimer oscillations. In the thick-film and thin-film regimes, we provide analytical expressions for the longitudinal conductivity, which highlight the interplay between electronic band topology and boundary-scattering in magnetotransport.

title: Multiscale wave-coupled neural networks for the inverse-design of broadband diffractive optics
summary: In this work, we introduce an inverse-design model called multiscale wave-coupled neural networks (MSWNets) inspired by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that integrate the deep-learning capability of fully-connected neural networks with rigorous Rayleigh-Sommerfeld diffraction theory. MSWNets are trained using spatial input and output functions describing the height profiles of diffractive structures. Importantly, a MSWNet is composed of multiple sub-networks that provide learning across multiple frequency components of the optimal design solution. First, we validate and analyze the inverse design capabilities of the MSWNets' architecture through training on the complete complex field propagated from the analytical design of an axilens, demonstrating accurate reconstruction. Finally, we employ MSWNets, trained to maximize focusing efficiency, for the inverse design of novel diffractive devices. In particular, we design and display the performance of several achromatic lenses and doublets across the mid-wave infrared region ($3-5\rm{\;μ} m$) with focal distance $f=500\rm{\;μm}$, demonstrating the potential of our inverse-design framework for the next-generation of broadband diffractive optical devices.

title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
summary: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
summary: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

title: A Candidate twin-spine photon model in MacCullagh's medium
summary: We model the vacuum as a rotationally elastic continuum, a low-energy electromagnetic approximation to the deformable spacetime metric of General Relativity. MacCullagh's single-parameter action yields the source-free Maxwell equations from resistance to twist, without separately postulating electric and magnetic fields. We show that a transversely localized field propagating rigidly at $c$ requires line defects; the minimal finite configuration is a twin-spine photon with two opposing displacement-current cores. It propagates without loss or transverse stress and admits linear and circular geometries with angular momentum $0$ or $\pm\hbar$. In a birefringent crystal, differential wave speeds reshape the shared spine trajectory, producing a continuous macroscopic torque without invoking superposed phase-delayed plane waves. For emission, we model the electron as a bound topological defect with a $π$-twist phase condition. Transverse acceleration shears its co-moving bow wave; the vacuum wave equation directs the residual dipole strain into twin-spine geometry, while the phase condition supplies a quantizing boundary condition. An accompanying SymPy Executable Research Record distinguishes postulated topology from derived mechanics.

title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
summary: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to $\textsf{QBlue}_{\texttt{BE}}$ by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a $94\%$ gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, including End Matter; Supplemental Material: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/caidish/KlayoutClaw
summary: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

title: Parallel Two-Photon Lithography: From Optical Nonlinearities to Energy Limits, Dose Control and Throughput Benchmarks
summary: Two-photon lithography (TPL) prints three-dimensional polymer architectures with sub-diffraction features, but writing them voxel by voxel limits its throughput. This review examines how parallelization overcomes this limit with fixed multi-focus arrays, reconfigurable holography using spatial light modulators and digital micromirror devices, hybrid metalens arrays, shaped beams, temporally focused projection and two-step absorption. An energy-deposition framework built on measured nonlinear absorption coefficients shows how the absorption order and coefficients of a resist determine its voxel size, energy per voxel and attainable voxel rate. Applied to parallel writing, the framework quantifies the costs of non-uniform foci, coherent crosstalk between foci, side-lobe losses in shaped beams and weaker axial confinement in projection. Published systems reach peak rates above $10^{8}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with scanned focus arrays and up to $1.7\times10^{9}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with grayscale projection under a fine-voxel definition, and parallel features as small as 20-55 nm. As rates rise, however, dose uniformity, proximity effects, heat, stitching and data bandwidth increasingly limit fidelity. A minimum reporting standard that includes the energy per voxel and sustained part-level rates is therefore proposed, together with priorities for the field: shared benchmark parts, predictive dose control and resists designed for parallel writing.

title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
summary: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.

title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moiré Interface Energetics and Mechanics
summary: The mechanical response of moiré interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moiré wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moiré periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.

title: Efficient phase-only wavefront shaping at 250 kHz for multimode fiber endomicroscopy
summary: Wavefront shaping through multimode fibers (MMFs) enables diffraction-limited fluorescence imaging with hair-thin probes, at a speed and light budget bounded by the wavefront modulator. Existing modulators provide at most two of three key characteristics: high refresh rate, (high) modal dimensionality, and light efficiency. Here, we demonstrate wavefront control through an MMF using a tailored phase-only microelectromechanical modulator that combines all three, with 8,192 elements arranged in a 32 x 256 array, 7-bit phase control, and a 250 kHz full-frame refresh rate. Direct on-axis phase modulation delivers 70+/-5% of the incident light into the modulated field and eliminates both off-axis encoding optical losses and hologram computation. The generated foci at the distal end of the fiber remain isotropic with high fidelity. We use singular-value decomposition analysis of the measured transmission to identify the effective degrees of freedom of our system. By scanning the focus at multiple depths, we demonstrate volumetric fluorescence imaging. These results open a new operating regime for adaptive in vivo multimode-fiber endoscopy.

title: Causal Consistency and Cost of Quantum Control
summary: An unknown quantum state can supply the information needed to control a computation, but how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action? We connect this resource question to causal consistency within the quantum state space. No-signaling requires identical observable predictions for remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input; quantum distinguishability then converts this requirement into finite-copy bounds. For amplitude amplification, we identify an exact low-copy obstruction and establish a dimension-independent, optimal quadratic dependence of the copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without reconstructing a classical state description. Prior knowledge of a real two-level family additionally permits exponentially decreasing error with the copy budget at fixed gain. These results separate the resources needed to perform a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction. The central connection is operational: physical consistency restricts which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information carried by its complete input determines the cost of doing so. This links a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.

title: Quantum Geometry Effects in Lattice Dynamics
summary: Quantum geometric effects such as the Berry curvature and the quantum metric are well established in electronic transport, whereas in lattice dynamics the Berry curvature also plays a key role: adiabatically following the lattice, electrons generate a molecular Berry curvature that splits degenerate optical phonons into chiral partners. To determine how the quantum metric affects phonons, we go beyond adiabatic lattice dynamics, identifying Berry curvature and quantum metric contributions to the electronic response of the lattice. Using first-principles calculations in the magnetic topological semimetal EuB$_6$, we find that phonon modes with chiral splitting and those with nonchiral splitting coexist. Unlike the former, which originate from the Berry curvature, the latter arise from the pure quantum metric, while the Berry curvature contribution is forbidden by crystal symmetry.

title: Optical Motion Sensing for Piezoelectric-Resonator-Based Power Converters
summary: Piezoelectric components present a promising alternative to conventional magnetics for miniaturized, high-frequency power converters. While high-Q piezoelectric resonators have demonstrated high efficiencies and large power densities in prototype high-frequency dc-dc converters, their optimal operating conditions are sensitive to temperature fluctuations and load variations. Therefore, robust closed-loop control is essential for practical deployment. Electrical approaches for sensing motional current may compromise the electrical isolation and electromagnetic interference (EMI) immunity inherently provided by the mechanical nature of these resonators. Here, we present an optical motion sensing approach for piezoelectric power converters. The optical sensing system comprises a laser, fiber optics, and a photodetector. The proposed approach uses optical interference to monitor the mechanical displacement in real time. The resulting optical signal carries both the amplitude and phase of the mechanical motion, which are necessary for closed-loop control. We experimentally characterize and validate this optical motion sensing approach using a 45-kHz piezoelectric resonator driven by a GaN half bridge with input voltages up to 45 V. We further experimentally demonstrate closed-loop control using the proposed optical motion sensing for a 99-kHz isolated piezoelectric converter. These initial results establish a viable pathway toward optically closed-loop control of piezoelectric power converters.

title: Coherent Control of Single-Photon Emission in Broadband Plasmonic Resonators
summary: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is challenging due to ultrafast relaxation induced by the broadband nature of the plasmonic near field. Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics theory, we demonstrate that an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field that is driven by a pulsed laser with frequency comb spectrum undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency comb components due to coherent accumulation, and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles with duration set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions are discussed for exponentially suppressing the probability of two or more emission events within the lifetime of the coupled emitter-nanocavity system. The spectral signatures of the optimal one-photon wavepackets are discussed. This work paves the way for the development of ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities.

title: Anatomy of orbital and spin responses in GaAs and Si: Hall, inverse Faraday, and magneto-optical Kerr effects
summary: Magneto-optical signals in nonmagnetic semiconductors entangle spin and orbital contributions, both in angular-momentum generation and magneto-optical detection. We calculate these contributions for electron-doped GaAs and Si using density-functional theory, linear-response theory, and a second-order density-matrix treatment of the inverse Faraday effect. At small electron doping, the intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity exceeds its spin counterpart in magnitude, while the orbital contribution to light-induced magnetization dominates over broad photon-energy ranges. We show that orbital- and spin-resolved optical Hall and polar Kerr coefficients exhibit stronger sensitivity to orbital moments than to equal spin moments. This contrast reflects direct electric-dipole coupling to orbital motion versus spin-orbit-mediated coupling to spin polarization. Consequently, Si maintains a substantial orbital magneto-optical response despite its weak spin-orbit interaction. At probe energies of 1.5 eV in GaAs and 3.0 eV in Si, the magnitude of the Kerr rotation per unit orbital moment is approximately 5 and 13 times larger than that per unit spin moment, respectively. Combining the calculated Hall conductivities and Kerr coefficients with a phenomenological drift-diffusion model yields predominantly orbital edge signals for the assumed diffusion constants and relaxation lengths. These results indicate that optical detection of induced magnetization in doped semiconductors such as GaAs and Si can be dominated by orbital signals, and therefore cannot be interpreted solely in terms of spin polarization.

title: Uniguided and unicoupled resonances in an asymmetric acoustic metasurface
summary: We theoretically study an acoustic metasurface that exhibits ultimate asymmetry in absorption under oblique incidence. This behavior arises from a counter-propagating pair of uniguided (UGR) and unicoupled (UCR) resonances. The UGR radiates to only one side, while the UCR radiates to both sides but can be excited from only one. In the lossless regime, the transmission phase winds by $2π$ across both UCR and UGR while the transmittance remains flat at any prescribed nonzero level. Thermoviscous losses introduce resonant intensity modulation and enable critical coupling, yielding perfect sound absorption exclusively for incidence through the channel that excites the UCR. Therefore, asymmetric metasurfaces with UCR and UGR offer a route to full phase control and perfect sound absorption.

title: photon number correlations in harmonics driven with classical and quantum light
comment: 13 pages (8 main, 5 supplemental), 8 figures (5 main, 3 supplemental), Submitted to Optics Express
summary: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised questions about whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour. Here, we compare the low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical and bright squeezed vacuum sources. The latter generates strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements show that the cross-correlations are fully classical and can be explained by the common fluctuations from the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed, which is well-explained by a click detector-response model.

title: Edge-asymmetric magnetism in semi-Dirac quantum dots
summary: In this study, we investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of quantum dots (QDs) throughout the transition from the Dirac limit to the semi-Dirac limit and beyond. When non-interacting semi-Dirac fermions are confined in triangular QDs, the resulting electronic states near the Fermi level are localized asymmetrically among the three edges of these systems. In the presence of electron interactions, we show that these low-energy states favor the formation of edge-asymmetric magnetism in triangular QDs. In particular, the magnetic moments were localized only along a single edge of the zigzag triangular QDs, corresponding to an edge-asymmetric ferromagnetic ground state. For various system sizes, these zigzag triangular QDs exhibit a one-unit increase in the ground-state total spin ($ΔS_z = +1$) beyond the semi-Dirac limit, revealing a striking result of this transition. In contrast, the remaining two edges are antiferromagnetically coupled in the armchair triangular QDs, indicating an edge-asymmetric antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state. We further identified the AFM ground states in hexagonal QDs, indicating that these types of asymmetric configurations are not unique to triangular QDs. Collectively, edge-asymmetric magnetism could create potential opportunities for future spintronics.

title: Acoustic bound states in the continuum in a labyrinthine meta-atom
summary: In this Letter, we theoretically and experimentally study acoustic bound states in the continuum (BICs) emerging in labyrinth meta-atom embedded in an acoustic waveguide. A symmetry-protected BIC is supported in the lossless limit when the meta-atom is positioned on the waveguide axis. Breaking the symmetry by shifting the meta-atom away from the center of the waveguide transforms the BIC into a radiative quasi-BIC, manifested by the emergence of a narrow resonant feature in the transmittance spectrum. The proposed concept is experimentally tested using a 3D-printed labyrinthine meta-atom placed inside an impedance tube. The measured transmittance spectra are consistent with numerical simulations and support the BIC-to-quasi-BIC transition induced by symmetry breaking in the presence of thermoviscous losses. The resonance frequency, contrast, and linewidth can be controlled by varying the meta-atom position. The observed behavior is interpreted within a two-mode temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT), providing an analytical description of the resonant response. The ability to tune radiative leakage in the presence of absorption makes the proposed acoustic BIC platform promising for the development of tunable absorbers, sensors, and modulators.

title: Subquantum Pilot-Wave System Theory: Structural and Amplitude Nonequilibrium under Source Fields
summary: A source in the Schrodinger equation changes the norm of the guiding wave, apparently conflicting with the conservation of probability. In source-extended de Broglie-Bohm dynamics the conflict disappears: probability is carried by the particle ensemble, while the wavefunction guides its motion. The difficulty is then different. What does quantum equilibrium mean when the particle distribution remains normalized but the guiding density does not? We show that the departure has two independent components: a structural one, measured by the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the particle distribution and the normalized guiding density, and an amplitude one, measured by the Born weight. The Born rule holds precisely when both are equilibrated. Their evolution is governed by the complex source-to-wavefunction ratio; scale covariance further distinguishes an independently prescribed source, against which the amplitude of the wave matters, from state-dependent generators for which rescaling remains a symmetry. We develop a source-aware analytical--computational method, combining exact or semi-analytical guiding fields with Bohmian trajectory transport, ensemble quadrature and independent numerical checks. Free-space impulses expose the limits of global diagnostics and an exact jump rule; a driven ring has constant Born weight but either periodic or secular structural departure; oscillators show both source-generated structural change and amplitude-only evolution, including a finite-horizon weak-drive plateau far below its frozen-particle value; and a coupled two-body model exhibits nonlocal guidance and evolving particle entanglement. The source-free, initially equilibrated sector recovers standard quantum mechanics.

title: Scanning nanowire quantum dot with radio-frequency read-out
summary: Scanning single-electron transistors (SETs) are highly sensitive local probes of charge and electric potential, but their integration with robust height control for scanning probe microscopy remains challenging. Furthermore, readout bandwidths are limited to tens of kHz, while characterizing faster charge dynamics is often of interest. Here, we present a scanning SET in the form of a nanowire (NW) quantum dot (QD) integrated at the apex of a non-contact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) cantilever. We demonstrate NC-AFM topographic imaging and local electrometry capability by mapping the electrostatic potential generated by a set of nanoscale voltage-biased gate electrodes. Comparison with electrostatic simulations shows agreement with the measured potential profiles. We demonstrate radio-frequency (rf) reflectometry read-out of the sensor, by embedding the QD in an LC-resonator. This platform establishes a route towards high-bandwidth scanning electrometry with simultaneous topographic contrast.

title: Reconfigurable Microwave Photonic All-Pass Filters based on Optical Kerr Microcombs
summary: Microwave photonic (MWP) all pass filters (APFs), which enable phase manipulation without altering signal amplitudes, are essential for phase engineering in high bandwidth microwave signal processing. However, achieving a high degree of reconfigurability in the filter order and characteristic parameters of APFs remains challenging for conventional methods. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a new strategy for realizing MWP APFs based on a microcomb driven transversal filter system, enabling high reconfigurability, sharp phase transitions with high group delays, and low loss. We experimentally demonstrate both 1st and 2nd order APFs, achieving a maximum amplitude variation (MAV) of 1.95 dB and a maximum group delay (MGD) of 580 ps for the former, and a MAV of 2.01 dB and an MGD of 1740 ps for the latter. In addition, both independent and joint tuning of APF characteristic parameters are demonstrated by simply programming the tap coefficients without changing any hardware, enabling highly reconfigurable filter response for diverse phase engineering functionalities. These results highlight the potential of our approach for implementing MWP APFs with both high performance and reconfigurability for practical applications requiring dynamic and versatile phase control.

title: Quantum nonclassicality as a marginal problem
summary: Classical explanations of quantum statistics---local, noncontextual, or causal---fail for one and the same reason: the probability distributions observed in different contexts are not the marginals of a single joint distribution. Every single context admits a classical model. This is Boole's problem of the "conditions of possible experience." Garg and Mermin treated it as a linear problem and showed, via Farkas's lemma, that its solvability is equivalent to a finite list of Bell-type inequalities, one for each extreme ray of a convex polyhedral cone; Pitowsky gave it the form of correlation polytopes. We sketch this common structure and discuss two examples: Aerts's elastic-band model, which reproduces the quantum cosine in one context but obeys the classical bound when contexts are combined; and nonclassicality in causal data fusion, where the contexts are supplied by interventions on a causal structure.

title: All-in-one Spintronic Sensory Neurons for Magnetic Edge Intelligence
summary: Magnetic fields enable non-contact sensing through nonmagnetic materials, offering opportunities for magnetic edge intelligence in autonomous recognition, navigation, and control. However, directly converting magnetic stimuli into neural spikes for local neuromorphic processing remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate an all-in-one spintronic sensory neuron (SSN) based on spin-transfer-torque magnetic tunnel junctions (STT-MTJs) fabricated using a 40-nm magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) process. By exploiting magnetic-field-modulated stochastic switching, the SSN enables probability-based sensing with an electrically tunable sensitive field window, allowing adaptive operation across different magnetic-field ranges without structural modification. This tunability alleviates the fixed sensitivity-range constraint of conventional tunneling magnetoresistance sensing, providing an accessible sensing range of +/-40 mT with an average probability sensitivity of 2.91%/mT. Importantly, the same stochastic switching process directly transduces magnetic stimuli into binary spike trains, integrating magnetic sensing, nonlinear rate encoding, and spike generation within a single nanoscale device. The resulting sigmoidal spike-rate response enables magnetic-field encoding, experimentally validated using the Neural Engineering Framework. Using experimentally characterized device responses, a simulated 10 x 10 SSN array achieves 90.7% accuracy in contactless magnetic-trajectory recognition with optimized encoding, approaching the software baseline. These results establish a scalable, MRAM-compatible approach to unifying programmable magnetic sensing and neural encoding for sensor-native edge intelligence.

title: 2D MXene integrated optical polarizers based on TiO2 with high performance
summary: Polarization control is essential for modern optical systems. Recently, two dimensional (2D) materials featuring highly anisotropic absorption across broad wavelength regions have emerged as a promising solution for realizing optical polarizers with operation bandwidths far exceeding those achievable using bulk materials. Despite this, existing 2D material based optical polarizers face critical limitations in simultaneously delivering high polarizer figures of merit (FOMs), robust power endurance, and scalable fabrication, hindering their practical deployment beyond laboratory. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by demonstrating optical polarizers through integrating 2D MXene films onto silicon photonic devices and subsequently converting them in situ into 2D titanium dioxide (TiO2). The 2D TiO2 exhibits significantly improved anisotropic absorption and thermal / chemical stability compared with MXene, enabling the hybrid polarizers to achieve a record high polarizer FOM of 17.5 (among 2D material-coated devices) and excellent power tolerance (stable under > 2 W coupled average power), together with a broad operation bandwidth (> 140 nm) and a high fabrication yield ( 98%). We also demonstrate microring resonator polarizers achieving high polarization extinction ratios up to 12 dB. With outstanding overall performance and strong capability for large-scale manufacturing, these polarizers represent a solid step towards industry ready implementations of 2D material based optical polarizers.

title: Revealing the Hidden Symmetry of the Asymmetric Quantum Rabi Model
summary: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear when the bias equals an integer multiple $m$ of the oscillator energy spacing. We trace the hidden symmetry to exchange between equal-energy partners $m$ rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders. Tunneling to other rungs makes this exchange vary in time. We construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation. At nonzero coupling and tunneling, the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. Spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence between the two opposite-parity states at a crossing. Its small-displacement exponent gives $m$, and its leading coefficient, together with the charge magnitude, predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.

title: Two-dimensional Thyristor
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer a viable platform for next-generation electronics beyond sub-3 nm nodes, yet essential nonlinear circuit elements, such as thyristors, remain unexplored on atomically thin platforms. Here, we report an atomically thin reconfigurable electro-optical thyristor based on a lateral WSe2-MoSe2-WSe2-MoSe2 PNPN heterostructure, directly grown via sequential edge epitaxy. Unlike single-junction 2D diodes, this multijunction architecture exhibits thyristor-like nonlinear switching, including forward blocking, abrupt snapback, bistability, and electrical latching. The device exhibits a forward-blocking voltage of 183 V, corresponding to a critical electric field of 1 MV/cm. Under open-gate conditions, avalanche-assisted carrier multiplication and regenerative feedback are associated with a sharp forward-voltage drop of 175 V, a pronounced current surge, and an ultralow holding voltage. Gate-pulse modulation and temperature-dependent measurements indicate avalanche-assisted thyristor operation and latching behavior. This 2D lateral heterostructure enables a new route to nonlinear and bistable switching, latching, ultralow standby power, and adaptive logic, opening the way for reconfigurable 2D electronics and photonic integrated circuits.

title: Polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling by Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum in bulk WS2 metasurfaces
summary: High-refractive-index dielectric metasurfaces supporting optical modes are ideal candidates for achieving strong coupling with transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) materials. However, optical illumination with a specific polarization is always required to estimate the maximal coupling strength in such coupled systems due to the polarization-dependent optical modes. Here, we propose a self-hybridized strong coupling between Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum (BZF-QBICs) mode and A excitons in the same bulk WS2 metasurface. By changing the thickness of the bulk WS2 metasurfaces, a typical anticrossing behavior with Rabi splitting of 165.9 meV is observed. Such Rabi splitting is unchanged when changing the polarization of the incident light from linearly to circularly polarizations, demonstrating the polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling. This work provides a novel method for realizing robust polarization-independent polaritons in bulk TMDCs metasurface and offers new insights for expanding the applications of polaritonic devices with arbitrary polarizations.

title: Phase-dependent atomicity and PPT edge states for cyclic-sign covariant qutrit maps
summary: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT). We obtain a necessary and sufficient criterion for decomposability in the entire seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on $M_3$. The criterion reduces to a one-variable inequality and, for positive maps in this class, characterizes indecomposability exactly. We apply it to a phase-dependent family obtained by adding a completely positive map to the Choi map. Every map in this family is positive, and we find the exact phase-dependent threshold for indecomposability and atomicity. At three phase values, the maps remain indecomposable for every finite deformation strength. Each indecomposable map gives an indecomposable entanglement witness through its Choi matrix. We construct PPT edge states of birank $(5,5)$ detected by these witnesses throughout the indecomposable region.

title: Aharonov-Bohm oscillations in transport through interacting quantum dots
summary: We investigate electronic transport through a two-terminal Aharonov-Bohm interferometer with two quantum dots in the presence of finite intra-dot Coulomb interactions. With the help of a diagrammatic technique, we derive, within linear perturbation theory in the tunnelling-coupling strength, analytic expressions for the occupations, current, and interferometric visibility in terms of a coherence measure that involves the sum of four off-diagonal elements of the reduced density matrix. The latter are calculated numerically from a master equation for arbitrary settings of the system parameters. For some symmetric setups, we obtain closed-form expressions for the linear conductance. We systematically analyse the impact of a finite Coulomb interaction on the interferometric visibility, and reveal a rapid suppression of destructive interference upon breaking of system symmetries. Our results are supported by alternative methods, including the TraSPI method.

title: Giant thermal transduction via feedback-phase engineering in a thin-film lithium-niobate opto-electro-mechanical oscillator
summary: Conventional resonant MEMS thermometry typically relies on the intrinsic temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF) of mechanical resonances. Here we show that embedding a suspended thin-film lithium-niobate mechanical resonator in an opto-electro-mechanical (OEM) feedback loop enhances the intrinsic coefficient by two orders of magnitude. By using laser--cavity detuning to control the loop's round-trip phase, and thus the Barkhausen-selected oscillation frequency, we engineer an effective TCF of $+1.24\times10^{4}$~ppm/K: a 100-fold enhancement and a sign reversal relative to its intrinsic TCF of $-124$~ppm/K. Temperature-dependent and open-loop phase measurements confirm that this giant response originates from feedback phase selection rather than from the passive resonator itself. This interpretation is further supported by the independently measured closed-loop oscillation frequencies and a detuning-dependent delay model. The same architecture also supports 2:1 subharmonic injection locking, yielding sub-6~Hz linewidths, reference-limited frequency stability, and tunable operation from $76.71$ to $76.82$~MHz. These results establish feedback-phase engineering as a general, post-fabrication route to both giant thermal transduction and low-noise yet tunable mechanical oscillation.

title: Many-Body Flux Selection in Chiral Quantum Batteries
summary: We study an interacting quantum-battery chain in which a synthetic flux controls interference between hopping paths. Keeping the internal battery Hamiltonian fixed, we seek the flux that leaves the most extractable work. Even a Gaussian reconstruction supplied with exact one-body information can rank competing flux settings incorrectly. A reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the finite systems and parameter ranges studied. Strikingly, the model can make an accurate control choice even when it excludes configurations carrying substantial probability in the exact state. Thus, choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state.

title: Interaction-driven ordering of multiple pseudospins and anomalous Hall metals in Bernal-stacked graphene
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures + Supplemental Material (4 pages, 1 figure)
summary: Recent observations of anomalous Hall states in Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene raise a fundamental question: How do electron-electron interactions organize multiple low-energy pseudospin sectors within each spin-valley flavor? Within the Hartree-Fock approximation, we analyze interaction-driven pseudospin ordering and spin-valley polarization as functions of displacement field and carrier density. We find a rich phase diagram shaped by the interplay between the two pseudospin doublets, including mixed flavor orders at charge neutrality and anomalous Hall metals upon doping. In particular, we identify topological states with $σ_{xy} \approx 6e^{2}/h$, consistent with recent experimental observations. Our results highlight the central role of multiple pseudospin doublets in the interaction-driven phases of even-layer Bernal multilayers.

title: Ultrabroadband, high-sensitivity time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy enabled by a Yb-based laser system
summary: Ultrafast optical fields have introduced numerous novel light-induced states in quantum materials. Identifying these states and elucidating their formation mechanisms require comprehensive, quantitative access to nonequilibrium electrodynamics across relevant energy scales. Here, we develop a Yb-laser-based time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy (TRTS) platform combining multi-pass-cell pulse compression, spintronic terahertz generation, and air-biased coherent detection. A single time-domain waveform scan provides continuous phase-resolved spectral coverage to 25 THz ($\sim$100 meV) with a Fourier resolution of 0.1 THz ($\sim$0.4 meV). This capability enables the characterization of both low-frequency charge dynamics and higher-energy resonant excitations in quantum materials under a common temporal reference. The system achieves a single-scan time-domain signal-to-noise ratio of 72 dB with long-term waveform stability, while preserving most of the laser pulse energy for tunable excitation. Measurements on intrinsic GaAs resolve extremely weak phonon features above 23 THz and demonstrate quantitative retrieval of equilibrium and transient complex optical properties. The resulting platform can provide a more complete microscopic picture of light-induced states in quantum materials.

title: Sharp Purity Based Entropy Bounds and Machine Learning Assisted Entropy Estimation
summary: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

title: Molecular Pawns on a Surface Chessboard: Computational Investigation of Nanographenes with Atomistic Methods
summary: Atomically precise nanographenes combine tunable electronic topology with localized, coherent spin states, making them candidate platforms for molecular quantum technologies.
